From the mighty Thames to the humblest brook, every stream has a hyporheic zone (HZ)—a
layer of sediment, small stones, and tiny creatures just below and alongside the streambed.
Stream water percolates into the HZ and mixes with upwelling groundwater, creating a unique
habitat “when the water from above meets the water from below” (as described in Ojibwe
traditional ecological knowledge). With its distinct water chemistry, temperature, and life-forms,
the HZ harbors great biodiversity, including microbes that play a key role in regulating organic
matter decomposition and other critical ecological processes.

prompt.text: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

content.text:
On account of its unusual ecology, the hyporheic zone is characterized by rare, highly
specialized species that are found neither in river water nor in groundwater.

By virtue of its transitional nature, the hyporheic zone sustains environmental conditions and
communities of organisms that are vital to the health of a river ecosystem.

While modern scientists have only recently recognized its importance, the concept of the
hyporheic zone has an established history in traditional ecological knowledge.

Because of its inaccessibility and its inhabitants’ microscopic size, the ecological significance
of the hyporheic zone has often been overlooked.
